Compilation never fails wholesale: an uncompilable mapping is skipped and recorded here, and
everything else still compiles.

Serializable but not deserializable: [`RejectReason`] is not, so neither is this.

oneOf.description:
One `event_<T>` / `object_<T>` view per declared type, plus `event`, `object`,

The `events`/`objects`/`e2o`/`o2o`/`object_attribute_changes`/`event_attr_meta` layout
`rust4pm`'s own reader (`DuckDbLinkedOCEL`) consumes. Unlike [`Self::PerType`], a type is

ExtractionCatalog.description:
The concrete, serializable [`Catalog`].

This is the form that crosses a bindings boundary, that an editor holds and sends back, and
that gets pinned to disk so a compile can be reproduced against a schema that has since

ExtractionError.description:
Why [`extract`](super::extract::extract) could not run at all, or a non-fatal problem
recorded in [`ExtractionReport::errors`] while it did.

Serializable but not deserializable: some variants carry `&'static str` fields (a borrow no
deserializer can manufacture), so this only ever crosses a bindings boundary outbound.

oneOf.description:
The blueprint failed [`validate`](super::validate::validate); `extract` refuses to run
it. Fatal.

A `Source` node names a `source_id` with no entry in the `providers` map `extract` was
given. Fatal.

A predicate's or split's regular expression failed to compile. Fatal; `validate` checks
this, so it should not happen when `extract` is called on a validated blueprint.

A `Join`'s `on` clause named a key column that its input's rows do not carry. Fatal:
dropping the column from the key instead would shorten it, silently turning the join into
a partial cross product.

column.description: The key column, as named on that side.

oneOf.description:
A [`RowProvider`](super::provider::RowProvider) call failed. Fatal: the rows a mapping
needs are simply not available.

node.description: The node being read when the failure happened.

oneOf.description:
An [`ExtractionSink`](super::sink::ExtractionSink) call failed for a reason other than a
policy below. Non-fatal: recorded and extraction continues.

context.description: What was being added when the failure happened.

oneOf.description:
Two mappings, or two rows, produced the same rendered id under two *different* types.
Only reachable under [`IdRendering::Raw`](super::blueprint::IdRendering::Raw). Non-fatal:
the row is dropped (see [`DropReason::IdTypeCollision`]) and the run continues. Merging
the two would silently fold two distinct entities into one, and writing this row's
attributes onto the other type's object used to abort the entire extraction.

requested_type.description:
The type this row wanted the id for. The type that already holds it is whatever the
sink reports for that id.

oneOf.description:
Two mappings declared the same attribute of the same entity type under different value
types. Non-fatal: the declaration is widened to a type that covers both (see
[`OCELAttributeType::coalesce`](crate::core::event_data::object_centric::OCELAttributeType::coalesce))
and every row is converted to that widened type, rather than the last declaration silently
winning while each mapping stored its own rows under the type *it* declared. Still worth
reporting: which type an attribute ends up with is then decided by a coincidence of two
mappings, not by either author's intent.

Deliberately does not name a mapping: a conflict is a property of the pair, and pointing
at whichever one happened to run second would be arbitrary. The type and attribute names
locate it precisely enough.

conflicting.description: The type the later declaration gave it.

declared.description: The type it was declared with first.

oneOf.description: `on_duplicate_object: Error` fired: `id` had already been added by `mapping`. Non-fatal.

mapping.description: The mapping whose row named the repeat.

oneOf.description:
`on_missing_endpoint: Error` fired: `endpoint` named `id`, which could not be resolved.
Non-fatal.

mapping.description: The mapping whose row named the endpoint.

oneOf.description:
`on_missing_endpoint: Error` fired for a sink that answered
[`Resolution::Deferred`](super::sink::Resolution::Deferred): the same policy violation as
[`MissingEndpoint`](Self::MissingEndpoint), reported once for the whole run instead of
once per endpoint. Non-fatal.

Such a sink detects the violation at [`finalize`](super::sink::ExtractionSink::finalize),
in bulk, where the mapping and the row that named the endpoint are long gone -- so this
deliberately names neither. It is emitted whenever
[`FinalizeReport::unresolved_endpoints`](super::sink::FinalizeReport::unresolved_endpoints)
is nonzero under that policy; without it, `Error` silently degraded to `Drop` for every
deferring sink.

count.description:
How many relations the sink could not resolve. Equals the number of
[`MissingEndpoint`](Self::MissingEndpoint) errors an eager sink reports for the same
run for an `E2O`/`O2O` endpoint or a `Target::Event`'s inline reference resolved via
[`resolve_object_endpoint`](super::mapping_exec::resolve_object_endpoint) --
**not** universally: an inline reference on a `Target::Event` whose own event this run
dropped is reported by an eager sink as [`DropReason::UnresolvedEndpoint`] on that
mapping, with no [`MissingEndpoint`] error pushed at all (there is no endpoint left to
resolve), while a deferring sink -- which cannot know at the call site that the event
will not exist -- stages the reference regardless and counts it here at finalize. This
count can therefore exceed the eager sink's `MissingEndpoint` tally by exactly that
many references.

ExtractionReport.description:
What [`extract`](super::extract::extract) produced, beyond the OCEL itself.

Serializable but not deserializable: [`ExtractionError`] carries `&'static str` fields (a
borrow no deserializer can manufacture), so this only ever crosses a bindings boundary
outbound, as a `#[register_binding]` return value.

errors.description:
Non-fatal problems collected while running -- a policy configured to error
(`on_duplicate_object: Error`, `on_missing_endpoint: Error`) or a sink failure on one
relation. Extraction continues past these; see [`ExtractionError`] for what aborts it
instead.

finalize.description:
What the sink did at [`ExtractionSink::finalize`](super::sink::ExtractionSink::finalize).

All zero for a sink that resolves relation endpoints eagerly, which reports everything
through [`per_mapping`](Self::per_mapping) instead. A sink that defers -- a path-backed
one, which cannot afford an in-memory id index -- reports its share of the same
information here, because it only learns it after the last row. See
[`Resolution`](super::sink::Resolution).

per_mapping.description:
One entry per mapping executed, in **desugared blueprint order** -- the order the author
wrote the mappings in, with each ordered group expanded in place. Deliberately not
execution order: execution is multi-pass and grouped by node (see
[`extract`](super::extract::extract)), so there is no single linear order to report, and
a diagnostic is far more useful indexed by what the author wrote. Each entry's
[`MappingRef::path`] names that authored entry outright.

rows_materialized.description:
The running total of rows every `Join`/`Union` materialisation this run performed
produced -- summed across materialisations, **not** a peak: a run that materialises two
nodes of a thousand rows each reports two thousand, even though the two never had to be
live at the same moment. It is an upper bound on peak buffered rows, not the peak itself.
(A cached materialisation is counted once, when it is computed, not again per reader.)

Includes the `Source`/`Filter` rows that fed a `Join`/`Union`, since those materialise
too the moment one needs them as an input; see invariant I1 on
[`extract`](super::extract::extract). Zero when no mapping's node graph contains a `Join`
or `Union`, since a pure `Source -> Filter` chain streams and never buffers a row past
the one being processed -- which is what makes zero here a meaningful witness that the
run streamed.

timing.description:
Where the run's wall-clock time went.

`None` from [`extract`](super::extract::extract) itself, which is handed a catalog and a
set of open providers and so has no idea what it cost to obtain them. The runner that owns
the connections fills this in; `process_mining_dbcon`'s does. Kept out of `extract` for a
second reason too: `std::time::Instant` panics on `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, and this crate
builds for wasm.

ExtractionTiming.description:
How long a run spent, split by phase, in milliseconds.

The split is the point: discovering a source's schema is a fixed cost paid before a single row
is read, and a caller that already holds a catalog can skip it entirely. Reporting one total
would hide which of the two a slow run actually spent its time in.

discovery_ms.description: Connecting to each source and reading its schema. Zero when the caller supplied a catalog.

extraction_ms.description: Reading rows and emitting entities: `extract` itself.

FinalizeReport.description:
What a sink did during [`ExtractionSink::finalize`], folded into
[`ExtractionReport::finalize`](super::report::ExtractionReport::finalize).

All zero for a sink that resolves eagerly ([`SlimOcelSink`](super::slim_sink::SlimOcelSink)):
it has nothing left to do at finalize, and everything it dropped or deduplicated is already
in the per-mapping counters. Nonzero entries mean the run used a deferring sink, and are
where that sink's share of the same information lives.

duplicates_removed.description:
Repeated entity ids removed at finalize -- a deferring sink's share of
[`MappingStats::deduplicated`](super::report::MappingStats::deduplicated), which it could
not detect while writing.

objects_created.description:
Objects synthesised at finalize under `on_missing_endpoint: Create`, for deferred
endpoints that turned out not to exist.

resolved_relations.description:
Relations written against a [`Resolution::Deferred`] endpoint that resolved to a real
entity at finalize.

unresolved_endpoints.description:
Relations whose deferred endpoint did not resolve. These are what a sink answering
immediately would have counted per mapping as
[`DropReason::UnresolvedEndpoint`](super::report::DropReason::UnresolvedEndpoint);
`on_missing_endpoint` decided what happened to them (dropped, or their object created).

IdRendering.description: How entity ids are rendered, for events and objects alike.

oneOf.description: Use the id expression's value verbatim.

Prefix the id with its type name, so ids from different types cannot collide.

Under this setting every relation endpoint must declare its type, since otherwise the
prefixed id cannot be rebuilt. Validation enforces that.

InlineObjectRef.description: An object related to an event declared by the same mapping.

anyOf.description: An instant with a fixed UTC offset, given as RFC 3339 text.

Literal.description:
A literal in a comparison or membership test.

Untagged in JSON, so `true`, `5`, `5.0` and `"x"` deserialize to the matching variant.
Order matters for `Boolean`, `Integer`, `Float` and `Text`, whose JSON shapes overlap only
with each other (a bare JSON boolean, number or string): boolean before integer before float
before text.

`Timestamp` is exempt from that ordering. It is deliberately not a bare string -- an
untagged variant added as `Timestamp(String)` would have the same JSON shape as `Text` and
would need placing *before* `Text` to ever be chosen, which would then make it swallow every
ordinary string that happens to parse as RFC 3339, silently reclassifying it. Wrapping it in
a single-field object instead (`{"timestamp": "..."}`) gives it a JSON shape distinct from
every other variant, so its position in this enum does not matter and no plain string is
ever at risk of being mistaken for a timestamp.

See [`Predicate::prepare`] for how a `Text` literal compared against a column of another
declared type is coerced -- that is the mechanism that makes a plain ISO-8601 string usable
against a timestamp column without needing this variant at all; this variant exists for a
blueprint author (or editor) that already knows it is authoring a timestamp.

Mapping.description: One mapping from a node's rows to entities.

label.description: Display label, also used to name this mapping in diagnostics.

node.description: The node whose rows this reads.

when.description: Only rows satisfying this produce anything. `None` accepts every row.

MappingEntry.description:
A mapping, or an ordered group of them.

`Single` is not boxed: it is the overwhelmingly common case, and callers construct and match
it directly.

oneOf.description: One independent mapping.

Mappings tried in order, where the first match wins.

Surface sugar: desugaring rewrites each guard to exclude the earlier ones, so nothing
downstream of validation sees this variant.

MappingRef.description: Points a diagnostic back at the mapping it came from.

index.description: Position in the desugared, flattened mapping list this run executed.

label.description: The mapping's own label, if it has one.

path.description:
The JSON path of the authored entry this mapping came from -- see
[`desugar_with_paths`](super::desugar::desugar_with_paths) -- so a diagnostic points at
what the author wrote rather than a position in the flattened list.

deduplicated.description:
Rows that tried to create an entity **the sink already had**. Not a loss: an object mapping
at event grain names the same object on every row by design. See
[`DuplicateObjectPolicy::Error`](super::blueprint::DuplicateObjectPolicy::Error) for what
turns a repeat into a loss instead.

# Exactly what is counted

One increment per row whose entity-creating call found the entity already present:

* a [`Target::Object`](super::blueprint::Target::Object) row whose
  [`resolve_object`](super::sink::ExtractionSink::resolve_object) answered
  [`Exists`](super::sink::Resolution::Exists), or whose
  [`add_object`](super::sink::ExtractionSink::add_object) was refused with
  [`SinkError::DuplicateObject`](super::sink::SinkError::DuplicateObject) -- the same event
  seen through an eager and a deferring sink respectively, which is why both report the same
  number;
* a [`Target::Event`](super::blueprint::Target::Event) row whose `add_event` was refused
  with [`SinkError::DuplicateEvent`](super::sink::SinkError::DuplicateEvent).

**Including a repeat across two mappings**, which is a change in meaning from "rows that
named an entity *this mapping* had already emitted". A second mapping naming an id a first
mapping created now counts one deduplication, where it used to count none. That distinction
needed one id set per mapping holding every id it named -- the last per-run structure whose
size tracked the data -- and it could never have been made to agree across sinks anyway: a
sink that answers [`Deferred`](super::sink::Resolution::Deferred) to every ask cannot say
whose object it already had.

# And what is not

**Resolving a relation endpoint is never counted**, so an `E2O`/`O2O` mapping reports zero
however often its rows repeat an id. Finding an endpoint that already exists is the normal
successful case, not a deduplication -- counting it made a healthy `E2O` mapping over `n`
rows report `n` deduplications (and `2n` for `O2O`) while nothing had been deduplicated at
all. Counting only the repeats among them is what the per-mapping id set used to buy, and it
went with it: a case-centric blueprint whose single event mapping creates its case objects
through an inline reference used to report `rows - distinct cases` here and now reports
zero. The objects are unaffected; only this counter is. A blueprint that wants that number
reported can name the cases with a [`Target::Object`](super::blueprint::Target::Object)
mapping, which is what [`FlatEventTable`](super::case_centric::FlatEventTable) already adds
as soon as there are case attributes.

dropped.description:
Rows dropped, by reason. A row that matches several reasons at once (rare) is counted
once, under the first one detected.

entities_emitted.description:
Entities or relations this mapping *handed to the sink*.

# Not "survived the run", for a sink that defers resolution

For an eager sink ([`SlimOcelSink`](super::slim_sink::SlimOcelSink)) the two coincide:
a relation whose endpoint does not exist is refused at the call site, so it is counted
under [`DropReason::UnresolvedEndpoint`] and never here.

A sink that answers [`Resolution::Deferred`](super::sink::Resolution::Deferred) --
[`DuckDbSink`](super::duckdb_sink::DuckDbSink) -- has no id index to refuse with, so the
relation is written, counted here, and only deleted at
[`finalize`](super::sink::ExtractionSink::finalize). The same dangling `E2O` therefore
reads as

| | eager | deferring |
|---|---|---|
| `entities_emitted` | 0 | 1 |
| `dropped[UnresolvedEndpoint]` | 1 | absent |
| [`FinalizeReport::unresolved_endpoints`](super::sink::FinalizeReport) | 0 | 1 |

This is the same reporting shift [`DuckDbSink`]'s own docs describe for `dropped`, seen
from the other side: the loss is reported in bulk at finalize because the mapping that
named the endpoint is long gone by then. Both logs still have the same contents.

To compare two sinks, or to count what a run actually produced, subtract
`ExtractionReport::finalize.unresolved_endpoints` from the run's total rather than
reading a single mapping's counter -- per-mapping attribution of a deferred loss does not
exist, by construction.

[`DuckDbSink`]: super::duckdb_sink::DuckDbSink

Inner-join two nodes on the given column pairs.

oneOf.description:
Concatenate the rows of several nodes, aligning columns by name.

This is `UNION ALL`, not `UNION`: duplicate rows are kept, because dropping them would
drop the entities they produce. The output columns are the union of the inputs' column
*names*, and an input that lacks one of them contributes `Null` for it rather than being
rejected -- so unioning two near-identical tables that differ by one column is legal.
Both rules are part of the model's semantics, not an implementation detail: a compiler
translating this node must emit `UNION ALL` with the absent columns explicitly
null-filled.

The object's type. Required under [`IdRendering::TypePrefixed`] and under

Two events claim one id. See [`Self::AmbiguousObjectIdentity`].

The underlying source failed while reading. Carries the backend's message rather than

RejectReason.description:
Why a mapping could not be compiled to a view.

Every variant names something the emitter refused to guess at. The three reasons the
redesign eliminated (`ConflictingPrefixFlag`, `DynamicTypeWithPrefixing`,
`SynthesizedChangeTableEventId`) are gone: prefixing is one blueprint-level policy, and
`ChangeTableEvents` no longer exists. [`RejectReason::DynamicTypeName`] narrowed from "the
type is dynamic" to "the type is dynamic *and no column domain was supplied*".

Serializable but not deserializable: several variants carry `&'static str` fields (a borrow no
deserializer can manufacture), so this only ever crosses a bindings boundary outbound.

oneOf.description:
A `Target::Event` with no `id` expression: the extractor mints a fresh `UUID` per row, a
nondeterministic side effect with no relational denotation.

A type name is read from the data and the catalog supplies no domain for the column it
comes from, so there is no name to put in `CREATE VIEW event_<T>`.

field.description: The position whose type is dynamic.

oneOf.description:
A column domain has more distinct values than [`MAX_TYPE_DOMAIN`], so a per-type shape
would emit one view per value.

column.description: The column the domain came from.

A mapping reads a node that is not declared.
A node's column shape could not be resolved -- typically an unknown source table.
The node graph contains a cycle, so there is no order in which to emit it.

node.description: A node id taking part in the cycle.

oneOf.description: A node has no columns, and SQL has no zero-column `SELECT`.
A `Union` node with no inputs.
An expression reads a column the node does not have.

The catalog's `col_type` for a column maps to no
[`ValueKind`](super::value::ValueKind), so the rule the extractor applies to that
column's values cannot be decided at compile time.

A column with no [`Value::canonical_string`](super::value::Value::canonical_string) --
`Float` or `Timestamp` -- is used at an identity position, where it makes the expression
`None` for every row.

A column whose [`Value::display_string`](super::value::Value::display_string) a SQL cast
does not reproduce -- Rust writes `1` where `DuckDB` writes `1.0`, and keeps a
timestamp's original offset -- feeds a position that reads it as text.
A timestamp is parsed by a `chrono` cascade that is not translated to SQL.

A join key column's declared kind is unknown, so whether the extractor's kind-tagged keys
can match is not decidable at compile time.

side.description: Which side the column is on.

oneOf.description:
A regular expression is not provably identical between Rust's `regex` crate (the
extractor) and RE2 (`DuckDB`).
A regular expression does not compile at all.

A `Template` has an unterminated or empty placeholder, which makes it `None` for every
row.

An attribute's declared type is not the source column's kind, and the coercion
`attribute_value` applies is not one a typed SQL column can reproduce -- its fallback on
failure is the cell's own natural value, which has a different type.

A mapping whose type name comes from the data declares an attribute that another mapping
declares under a different type. A statically-named type has its declarations reconciled
before the first row; a data-named one declares lazily, one row at a time, so which type
wins depends on row order.
The requested [`EmissionShape`] is not implemented.

A relation view's dependencies on other relation views form a cycle, so no order exists
in which its `CREATE VIEW` (or CTE, or `CREATE TABLE ... AS`) could run. Not reachable
from a [`validate`](super::validate)d blueprint -- see the note on
[`CompiledOcel::relations`] -- so this only guards a blueprint fed to [`compile`]
unvalidated.

The blueprint does not [`validate`](super::validate::validate) against the catalog, so
nothing was compiled at all. One per [`ValidationError`](super::validate::ValidationError),
rendered through its `Display`: that type is not `Deserialize`, and neither is this enum,
so carrying it structurally would buy nothing a caller could read back.

SinkError.description:
Why an [`ExtractionSink`] call failed.

Serializable but not deserializable: [`SinkError::UnknownType`] carries a `&'static str` (a
borrow no deserializer can manufacture), so this only ever crosses a bindings boundary
outbound, nested inside [`ExtractionError::Sink`](super::report::ExtractionError::Sink).

oneOf.description: [`ExtractionSink::add_event`] was called with an id already present.
[`ExtractionSink::add_object`] was called with an id already present.

[`ExtractionSink::add_object`] was called for `id`, but `id` is already present under a
*different* object type -- only reachable under
[`IdRendering::Raw`](super::blueprint::IdRendering::Raw). Distinguished from
[`SinkError::DuplicateObject`] because the two must not be handled alike: a plain repeat
means "the id already exists, append to it", while this means two distinct entities
collided on one id. A sink that cannot tell the two apart at
[`resolve_object`](ExtractionSink::resolve_object) time -- because it defers, and
therefore never answers `Missing` for a type mismatch the way an eager sink's `resolve_object`
does -- returns this from `add_object` instead, once the attempted insert makes the
mismatch unambiguous.
